results.corrected_extracted: A single-author review searching 1990 to 2004, with earlier studies also included for symptoms the 1990 review had left unclear: more than 3,500 citations, 792 abstracts read, 290 articles read and 120 cited; inclusion required published prospective studies of cigarettes with more than 18 hours of abstinence; the author chose which results to include on his subjective opinion of rigor, consistency and size, and states that data collection and interpretation rested solely on his judgments.
results.note: All counts and criteria match. But pp. 316-317 say depression, drowsiness, fatigue and physical symptoms were reviewed from all studies, before and since 1990; 4 of the 15 core studies (Table 1) predate 1990.

p. 318 and Table 1 (p. 317) match: 15 studies, n 11 to 178; all but one pre-quit values; n=9 RCT control arms; n=2 control groups, 2 generalizable, 3 over 90 (symbol checked on render), 5 low attrition; no meta-analysis.

Counts match pp. 318-319 (anger 7/1/2; dysphoria 6 cited, 2 not, Hillemann fall). West 1991, also in Table 1, is cited separately as rising. Author also calls anger duration unclear and judges dysphoria a true but less reliable symptom.

results.corrected_extracted: Difficulty concentrating peaked in the first few days and lasted from a week or less to 4 weeks or more; impatience rose for 3 to 4 weeks or more in all 3 newer studies; sleep fragmentation (waking at night) increased consistently in sleep-EEG and clinical studies lasting 5 to 14 days, with more recall of vivid dreams; restlessness peaked on days 1 to 3 and lasted 2 to 4 weeks (1 week in one study).
results.note: All else matches pp. 319-322. Restlessness paragraph (p. 322) adds that one study (Ward, Swan et al., 2001) found a duration of 1 week; added so the range is not overstated.

pp. 320-322 match: alertness 2 down, 2 up, 3 no change; fatigue no effect in 3 of 4; all negative for headache, sweating, heart racing, tremor, rash; dizziness 2 vs 1; constipation, cough, mouth ulcers one study each.
p. 322 matches, including 38% and 61%. The author hedges, calling the exact duration unclear and 2-4 weeks 'Perhaps the most accurate statement' (stated flatly in the abstract).

p. 27 matches: searches ended 31 May 2011, English, from 2004 (earlier studies via the 2007 review); randomized crossover or parallel, at least 2 h abstinence; studies of people in cessation programmes or on NRT excluded.

p. 29 matches: 19 RCTs, 7 parallel, 12 crossover; 14 published, 4 PhD and 1 MSc theses; 10 to 84 participants; 5 to 40 minutes; all controls passive; immediately after or 5 minutes after in three studies [45,49,53].
Checked on rendered pp. 30 and 32. Observations 797 and 837 from p. 30 and Tables 2-3. Table 2 prints n = 16 studies for this SoD analysis against 15 in the text and Figure 2.
Rendered p. 32 matches Tables 2-3; text gives the one-stage SoD lower limit as -2.53 (Table 2: -2.52). Mid-ranges recomputed: -1.89 +/- 1.96 x 0.850 and -2.03 +/- 1.96 x 0.722.

results.corrected_extracted: Every study favoured exercise, from −0.22 to −4.54 points for strength of desire; the three studies that included isometric exercise had among the smallest effects, with intervals including zero in two of them for strength of desire (−0.55 and −0.22), and the largest effect came from the study with the highest baseline craving.
results.note: Figures checked on render. Authors say isometric studies had 'the smallest' effects, but in Figure 2 Daniel 2004 cycling (-0.93) is below Haasova 2011 (-0.94), whose PA arm pooled walking with isometric exercise.

Confirmed; the methods' second stage and the results also use the standardized label. Own check: 14 of 15 Figure 2 effects lie between raw post and change differences of Table 1 means (Daniel 2004: -0.93; standardized about -0.49).

results.corrected_extracted: Titles were screened by the first author alone; quality was reported only as randomization (one study allocated by recruitment order); the review was paid for from internal institutional funds, and the authors report no connection with the tobacco or pharmaceutical industries; editors' count from the reference list and the text: 17 of the 19 included trials list at least one of the review's authors.
results.corrected_locator: Results › Literature search (p. 28); Study characteristics and quality assessment, 4th paragraph (p. 30); Declarations of interest (p. 35); References 27-29 and 39-67 (pp. 36-37)
results.note: Count recomputed: 17/19 (only Katomeri [27] and Thompson [28] list none); the unpublished trial's authors are named on p. 28. Interests now as printed (tobacco or pharmaceutical industries).

Abstract and pp. 115-116 match (27 studies; 12 included: 8 gum, 3 inhaler, 1 microtab, no lozenge; first week only). The criteria list omits one of five: a clearly abstinent or nearly abstinent sample.

p. 117 text and Table 3 agree: inhalers 3/3, microtab 1/1, gum 3/7 (Gross and Stitzer, Hughes 1991, Fagerstrom).

p. 117 matches. The text's 'In most studies' lapsers were included conflicts with Table 2, where only 5 of 12 trials included them.

Table 1 and text (pp. 108-109) match on the page images. The word heavy is the editors' gloss: criteria were at least weekly use plus a minimum amount over 3 months. Raters were mainly the first author.

results.corrected_extracted: Craving was absent in the late crash and during heavy sleep; over 80% used sedatives (including alcohol or opiates) at least once to sleep; five people whose ordered cocaine arrived 2 to 5 hours after their last dose did not use it; eight people described a crash of at most 3 days and the rest up to 6 days, while the figure gives 9 hours to 4 days.
results.note: Numbers match the p. 111 image and the figure. The paper says 'sedative agents (including alcohol or opiates)', so other sedatives are not excluded.

results.corrected_extracted: All people with other diagnoses and four others were treated with medication, so the later phases were not observed without it in most; the authors call the findings preliminary, limited by small numbers and the lack of structured instruments or blind observation in parts of the study; editors' count: 20 of the 30 took medication.
results.note: p. 112 image matches; count recomputed: 16 with diagnoses (Table 2) plus 4 = 20 of 30. The authors limit missing instruments and blinding to parts of the study; diagnoses used structured interviews.

results.corrected_extracted: In a controlled residential study, all the men with cocaine dependence reported last using cocaine within 48 hours before admission; mood distress and craving were highest on admission day and fell over the 28 days (craving F = 17.270, P<.01); sleep reports did not differ from controls except more difficulty falling asleep and a greater improvement in clear-headedness on arising.
results.corrected_locator: Results › Subject Characteristics, 3rd paragraph; Figure 1; Outcome › Mood Scores, Craving for Cocaine and Self-reports of Sleep (p. 864); Figure 2 and Table 2 (p. 865)
results.note: Values match Table 2 and Fig. 2. Controls were men too and used no cocaine; the abstract and p. 864 name clear-headedness on arising as a second sleep difference. Locator adds Figure 1 and Self-reports of Sleep.
Checked on pp. 862-863 images: 30, 16, 14, 12; 10 controls; days and 9 AM to noon; route 10 intravenous, 1 smoking, 1 intranasal; antisocial personality disorder 58% vs 0% (chi-square 10.10).
Table 2 (p. 865 image) matches: all these effects P<.01 except the total mood distress group effect (P<.05); craving F = 17.270, df 10,110.

results.corrected_extracted: Sleep reports did not differ from controls except more difficulty falling asleep in the cocaine group throughout (group F = 10.428) and a greater improvement in clear-headedness on arising in the cocaine group (interaction F = 2.001); the other sleep measures improved over time in both groups; weight gain of 4.6 kg against 3.8 kg did not differ; heart rate rose 10.9 beats a minute in the cocaine group and fell 2.3 in controls.
results.note: Values match pp. 864-866 and Table 2. Added the clear-headedness group-by-time interaction (2.001, P<.05), which the abstract and the Fig. 3 legend also report as a group difference.
p. 866 Comment matches, including 'not cyclical or phasic' and the controlled-environment explanation.

p. 867 matches. The authors also name the antisocial-disorder confound, extra staff time for the cocaine group, unverified cannabis use and no EEG sleep studies.
p. 111 image and figure match (1 to 5 days, 1 to 10 or more weeks, figure 1-10 wk; failure within several days of phase 2).
Abstract, p. 2 and p. 5 match (9 studies, N = 246; 9927 nonduplicate records; 167 full texts; through March 2015).
p. 3 matches. Page 9 adds that no study reported the needed statistics, so r = 0.5 was in effect assumed throughout; the authors say this biases effects toward zero.
Negatives checked on rendered p. 6 and Table 3 (b = 0.05, P<.001). Table 1's efficiency rows sum to N = 159, not the text's 155 (Giblin and Strobel listed as 16, not 12).

Checked on the rotated Table 1: ranges and signs match; ages 102 to 139.2 months. The table omits the total-sleep-time heading; its last seven rows match N = 223.
pp. 8-9 match. The paper also prints no financial relationships and no potential conflicts of interest for the authors.

p. 517 matches; the rash affected two patients and was the only event judged study-related.

Footnote (p. 512), Medication and Statistical Analysis (p. 515) and Disclosure (p. 518) match; other authors declared none. The observed 16-minute difference is about half the planned detectable change, with 19 analysed.

Rendered p. 516 matches all values; a further 4% were minimally worse. The 0.67 is an uncontrolled pre-post effect over all children in this phase.
Abstract and p. 515 match (33 - 5 - 5 = 23). The no-control-group statement is the editors' reading of the design (p. 514, Fig. 1). The t(28) df implies 29 children, a third count.

plain.fix: short: After stopping smoking, people can feel grumpy, anxious and restless, and wake more at night, for weeks.
plain.note: The word often implies a frequency the review does not give (its own limit line says so); the finding is more waking than before quitting. Other lines match pp. 315-322.

plain.fix: how 1: 19 small studies compared a short bout of exercise with sitting quietly; most tested the same people both ways.
plain.note: 12 of the 19 were crossover trials, so most did not compare different people. How 2 holds for point estimates; two intervals included zero, which its by-a-little wording covers.

plain.fix: how 1: 12 studies compared nicotine products with dummy products; in one study the comparison was a low-nicotine gum.
plain.note: West et al. (1984) compared against low-nicotine gum, not a nicotine-free dummy (Table 2, p. 118). Other lines match Table 3 and the acknowledgement.

plain.fix: how 3: Some people had passing thoughts of suicide, which were limited to the crash.
plain.note: The added clause is advice not in the paper; a help pointer, if wanted, belongs in the site's safety box (senior author's call). The paper reports suicidal ideation (43% of 14), which thoughts of dying understates.

plain.fix: how 1: The men were compared with 10 men with no history of drug problems, living in the same unit. | how 3: Their reported sleep was much like the other men's, except that falling asleep was harder and feeling clear-headed on waking improved more.
plain.note: Controls had no history of drug abuse or dependence, but 30% smoked and 2 had cannabis-positive urine; clear-headedness was a second group difference. How 2 is a fair reading of Figures 1 and 2.

plain.fix: short: On stimulant medicine, children took longer to fall asleep and slept less than on nights without it, sleep monitors showed. | how 4: In studies where children had taken the medicine for longer, the effect on the share of time in bed spent asleep looked smaller, but this does not prove sleep gets better.
plain.note: The short line needs its comparison. Time on medication moderated only sleep efficiency (Table 3), not latency or total sleep (Tables 2 and 4).

plain.fix: how 3: Reported health problems were mild or moderate, apart from one severe migraine, and about as common with the dummy pill.
plain.note: Safety (p. 517): one severe migraine; no event was judged related to melatonin. The 16 minutes matches the diary means (62.1 vs 46.4) and the abstract.

plain.fix: short: With a set bedtime routine, children on ADHD medicine fell asleep sooner than before, but most still took a long time.
plain.note: The comparison is with their own earlier sleep. How 3's figure of about 28 is fair: the abstract prints 27 and the participant flow implies 28.
